title: They Went to America for Better Jobs. Now They’re Coming Home to Fewer Ones.
excerpt: Indian tech hiring has fallen to a 28-month low just as thousands of H-1B professionals are returning. The market that was supposed to catch them isn’t ready.
body:
For years, India’s tech professionals treated the H-1B visa as the golden ticket — a one-way path to Silicon Valley salaries, American mortgages and a permanent seat at the global table. The return ticket was supposed to be optional. In 2026, it isn’t.

New data from staffing firm Xfino shows that active technology job openings in India have dropped to 93,000 in June — a 14 percent fall from the previous month and the lowest level in 28 months. At the same time, roughly 7,300 Indian tech workers have returned from the United States in the first half of 2026 alone, pushed out by layoffs, rising visa fees and a political climate that has made the H-1B programme more hostile than at any point in its three-decade history.

The gap between the two numbers is the story.

## The Push and the Pull

The forces driving Indian professionals out of America are by now well documented. More than 100,000 US tech workers have been laid off this year, with an estimated 25,000 of them on H-1B visas. The Trump administration has proposed a $100,000 fee for new H-1B applicants, floated plans to cut the post-graduation grace period for F-1 students from 60 days to 30, and launched a broader overhaul that US Ambassador Sergio Gor insists is “not specifically directed at India” — even as Indian workers account for 71 percent of approved H-1B beneficiaries.

At least a dozen Republican lawmakers have backed four separate bills this year to restrict, suspend or eventually eliminate the programme entirely. One proposal from Texas Representative Chip Roy would slash the maximum H-1B stay from six years to two and require workers to prove they intend to leave.

The result is a climate of compounding uncertainty. “For anyone who already has a master’s degree, they are not going to be able to go back and say, ‘I need another master’s degree because I need work authorisation to continue working,’” said Danielle Goldman, co-founder and CEO of Build, referring to the potential narrowing of the Day 1 CPT pathway that thousands of Indian graduates have relied on after repeated H-1B lottery rejections.

## Coming Home to a Locked Door

But the harder reality is what awaits on the other side. India’s domestic tech sector has been shedding jobs and freezing hiring since 2022, with over 30,000 cuts reported in the last four years. The IT services industry — once the guaranteed fallback — is shrinking its bench strength as generative AI automates entry-level coding, testing and support roles.

“After the hiring buoyancy of 2021, the Indian tech sector has not had a period of stability extending beyond a quarter,” said Kamal Karanth, co-founder of specialist staffing firm Xpheno. “Considering the current dynamics, it is definitely not the best of times for US-settled H-1B talent to return to India.”

Returnees face a triple mismatch. Their salary expectations — calibrated to Bay Area cost-of-living — are often three to five times what Indian employers are willing to offer for equivalent roles. Their experience, shaped by large-scale American product engineering, doesn’t always translate to the client-services model that still dominates India’s IT industry. And Indian employers are openly sceptical that returnees will stay, fearing they’ll jump back to America at the first opportunity.

“The companies will either struggle because they won’t have the talent or they will have to get creative and find alternate solutions,” Goldman said. But in India, the creativity is running in the opposite direction: employers are quietly passing over US returnees for candidates who never left.

## The GCC Lifeline

There is one bright spot, and it has three letters: GCC. Global Capability Centres — the in-house technology arms that companies like JPMorgan, Google and Goldman Sachs have built in Bengaluru, Hyderabad and Pune — are among the few employers actively hiring senior talent with US experience.

Raja Lahiri, a partner at Grant Thornton Bharat, said that while demand in traditional IT services has weakened, there is “massive opportunity for AI skills, and the demand is only going to increase.” Professionals with over a decade of experience in a single domain — particularly AI, machine learning and cloud architecture — are the likeliest to land on their feet.

But GCCs employ a fraction of India’s tech workforce. For the majority of returnees, the arithmetic is grim: a shrinking US pathway on one side and a saturated Indian market on the other.

## A Structural Shift, Not a Blip

The numbers point to something larger than a cyclical downturn. Xfino projects that by the end of 2026, the number of Indian tech workers returning from the US will outpace those leaving for the first time. China, sensing an opportunity, has rolled out a K-visa programme that does not even require employer sponsorship — a deliberate contrast to the H-1B’s lottery system.

India’s own hiring data tells a structural story. Analysis by the Pahle India Foundation shows that employment growth in the tech sector is “increasingly tilted toward workers with experience, while those at the entry level face a slowdown.” AI is not eliminating jobs overnight, but it is changing who gets hired — and mid-career returnees from the US, with their high salary floors and narrow specialisations, are finding themselves on the wrong side of the shift.

The traditional model — study in India, migrate to the US, settle permanently — is being replaced by something more cyclical, more uncertain and, for many, more painful. For the 7,300 who have already come home this year, the question isn’t whether they’ll find work. It’s whether the India they return to has room for the careers they built.

## What It Means for the Diaspora

For the roughly four million Indian tech professionals in the United States, the message is stark: the safety net has holes on both sides. Those clinging to the H-1B path face rising fees, political hostility and an annual lottery that rejects the majority of applicants. Those considering a return face a domestic market that treats US experience as a liability as often as an asset.

Financial advisors in the diaspora community are increasingly recommending that professionals maintain dual-country savings, avoid over-leveraging on American mortgages, and build India-facing professional networks before they need them — not after. The era of the one-way ticket may be ending. The question is whether India’s economy is ready for the people coming home.

*Sources: Xfino, Xpheno, Grant Thornton Bharat, The Indian Eye, Outlook Business, AInvest, The Hindu BusinessLine, Livemint*
